subject: Science
board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Biology (4BI1) and Chemistry (4CH1)
source: Edexcel IGCSE 4BI1/4CH1 specification summary (content/syllabus/ks4/gcse-science.json), Y10 units Biology 1, Biology 2, Chemistry 1, Chemistry 2. Drive material not used. Not re-taught because covered by the existing UK-GCSE-based lessons in content/lessons/gcse-science/y10.json: animal, plant and bacterial cell structure and levels of organisation, specialised cells, differentiation and stem cells, enzymes with temperature and pH and the active site, food tests, diffusion, osmosis and active transport (Biology 2 points 1-3 mostly); states of matter and changes of state, purity and melting points, mixtures and separation, chromatography and Rf, atomic structure and isotopes, relative atomic mass, Periodic Table groups, periods and electronic configurations (Chemistry 1 points 1-4 mostly). Gaps remain in solubility curves and gas diffusion, which are taught here.

lessons.unit: Biology 1: The nature and variety of living organisms
lessons.title: Characteristics of living organisms and the eukaryote groups
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes something alive, and how do biologists sort the living world?
objectives: State the eight characteristics of living organisms
Describe the features of plants, animals, fungi and protoctists
Classify an organism from a description of its cells and nutrition
successCriteria: All: name the characteristics and the four eukaryote groups
Most: describe the key features of each group with an example
Some: classify an unfamiliar organism and justify using evidence
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: biodiversity across habitats
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the variety of life; stewardship (khilafah) means caring for what we classify

keywords.def: organism whose cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
mostly single-celled eukaryote that is not a plant, animal or fungus, e.g. Amoeba
removal of toxic waste and substances in excess of requirements
taking in materials for energy, growth and development

starter: Bismillah. Name two structures found in plant cells but not animal cells.
What is the function of the nucleus?
In which organelle does aerobic respiration take place?

teach.heading: Eight characteristics of life
bullets: Every living thing shows all eight, at some point
Use them as a checklist for 'alive or not?'
teach.note: Ask pupils to shout out a verb for each: move, respire, sense, control, grow, reproduce, excrete, feed. Stress that excretion is not the same as egestion (removing undigested food). Check against the specification wording for the eighth characteristic (control of internal conditions) before printing.

head: Characteristic
Meaning
Example
rows: action causing a change of position or place
a plant leaf turning to the light
chemical reactions in cells releasing energy from nutrients
keeping conditions in the body steady
permanent increase in size and dry mass
making more of the same kind
removing toxic waste or excess substances
taking in materials for energy and growth

teach.heading: The four eukaryote groups
bullets: All eukaryote cells have a nucleus
Groups differ in cell walls, chloroplasts and feeding
teach.note: Walk across the table row by row. Ask: which feature separates fungi from plants? (chitin walls, no chloroplasts, absorb food). Point out that protoctists are a mixed group and that Chlorella has chloroplasts but is not a plant because it is single-celled.

head: Group
Cell wall
Chloroplasts
Nutrition
Examples
rows: feed on other organisms; store glycogen
absorb nutrients from dead or living matter

teach.heading: Model: classify the organism
bullets: Look for cell wall material first
Then chloroplasts, then how it feeds
teach.note: Think aloud: match each clue to the table. Ask pupils which single clue would be enough to rule out 'plant' (no chloroplasts).

model.problem: Organism X is multicellular. Its cells have nuclei and cell walls made of chitin, no chloroplasts. It grows as thread-like hyphae through stale bread and absorbs nutrients. Which group is it?
steps: Nuclei, so it is a eukaryote
Chitin wall and no chloroplasts rules out plants
Hyphae and absorbing nutrients is typical of fungi
Mucor is a fungus that grows on bread
model.answer: Fungus (e.g. Mucor)

teach.heading: Common error: fungi are plants
bullets: Fungi were once grouped with plants
They do not photosynthesise
teach.note: Ask where a mushroom gets its energy. Many pupils think fungi 'grow in soil like plants'.

misconception.wrong: A mushroom is a plant because it grows from the ground.
misconception.right: Fungi have chitin cell walls and no chloroplasts, and absorb nutrients from dead matter, so they are not plants.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
Show on three, then explain
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils see 'chloroplasts' and say plant. Chlorella is single-celled and classified as a protoctist.

check.q: Chlorella is a single-celled organism with a nucleus and chloroplasts. It is best classified as:
check.why: It has a nucleus, so it is a eukaryote; being single-celled with chloroplasts places it with the protoctists. Plants are multicellular and prokaryotes have no nucleus.

practice: A mushroom grows on a log, takes in nutrients, releases spores and grows larger over a week. Which characteristics of life does it show?
Mucor has hyphae and no chloroplasts. Amoeba is single-celled and moves by pseudopodia. State one feature that is the same and one that is different.
Explain why a flame is not classed as living even though it grows and uses oxygen. [3 marks]
independent: Core: Copy and complete a table giving cell wall, chloroplast and nutrition for plants, animals, fungi and protoctists.
Extend: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. Explain why it is not a protoctist. [3 marks]
Stretch: A student says a crystal growing in a saturated solution is alive because it grows. Evaluate this using all eight characteristics.
exit: Name the four groups of eukaryotes. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: give two characteristics a car engine shows and two that it does not.
lessons.homework: Revise the table of eukaryote groups; make 8 flashcards for the characteristics.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded characteristic cards with picture prompts. Stretch: ask why viruses are debated as living.

lessons.unit: Biology 1: The nature and variety of living organisms
lessons.title: Prokaryotes, pathogens and viruses
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a medicine kill bacteria but not a virus?
objectives: Describe the features of bacteria as prokaryotes
Name the four types of pathogen with an example disease each
Describe viruses as non-living particles
successCriteria: All: name pathogen types and a disease each
Most: describe bacterial and viral structure
Some: compare sizes and explain why antibiotics fail against viruses
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: hygiene and preventing infection
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: tahara (cleanliness) as protection of health; gratitude for the body's defences

keywords.def: single-celled organism with no nucleus; DNA free in the cytoplasm
organism that causes disease
small circle of DNA found in bacteria
non-living particle with genetic material in a protein coat; reproduces only inside host cells

starter: Bismillah. List the four eukaryote groups.
State two features of a eukaryotic cell.
Convert 3 mm to micrometres.

teach.heading: Bacteria: prokaryotes
bullets: Single-celled, no nucleus
Circular chromosome plus small plasmids
Cell wall, cytoplasm, cell membrane
teach.note: Show a labelled bacterium. Ask what is missing compared with an animal cell (nucleus, mitochondria). Mention that some bacteria are useful (Lactobacillus makes yoghurt) and some harmful (Pneumococcus causes pneumonia).

left.title: Bacterium (e.g. Lactobacillus, rod-shaped)
points: No nucleus; DNA loose in cytoplasm

teach.heading: Four types of pathogen
bullets: A pathogen is anything that causes disease
Each type can infect humans
teach.note: Ask pupils to guess how each spreads. Malaria: the pathogen Plasmodium is carried by Anopheles mosquitoes (the vector).

teach.heading: Viruses are not cells
bullets: Genetic material inside a protein coat
No cytoplasm, no nucleus, no respiration
Only reproduce inside a host cell
teach.note: A virus shows reproduction only when inside a host, so it is described as non-living. Examples: tobacco mosaic virus (plants), influenza, HIV.

model.problem: A bacterium is 2 µm long. An influenza virus is 100 nm across. How many times longer is the bacterium?
steps: Convert to the same unit: 2 µm = 2000 nm
Divide: 2000 ÷ 100
model.answer: 20 times

teach.heading: Why antibiotics do not work on viruses
bullets: Antibiotics target bacterial cell processes
Viruses live inside our own cells and have none
teach.note: Link forward to the antibiotic resistance lesson in Year 11. Pupils often say antibiotics 'fight infections'; be precise.

misconception.wrong: Antibiotics cure all infections, including colds and flu.
misconception.right: Antibiotics kill bacteria only. Colds and flu are caused by viruses, which have no bacterial structures to target.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: 'reproduces on its own' sounds alive; insist that a virus has no cell and replicates only in a host.

check.q: Which statement about viruses is correct?
options: They reproduce on their own in water
They have a cell wall and cytoplasm
They reproduce only inside host cells
check.why: Viruses have no cellular structure and replicate only in a host cell, so they are described as non-living particles.

practice: Name the pathogen type for malaria and for athlete's foot.
Draw and label a bacterium with four parts.
A bacterium is 3 µm long and a virus is 60 nm. How many times longer is the bacterium?
independent: Core: Make a table of the four pathogen types with an example and disease.
Extend: Compare a bacterial cell and a virus in four points. [4 marks]
Stretch: Explain why an antibiotic given for a viral infection would be harmful as well as useless.
exit: Why are viruses not classed as living organisms? [2 marks]
Return to the big question in one sentence.
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word explanation for a younger pupil of why viruses are not living cells.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: labelled diagram bank. Stretch: research how TMV was discovered.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Photosynthesis and limiting factors
lessons.bigQuestion: What stops a plant from photosynthesising faster?
objectives: Write word and balanced equations for photosynthesis
Describe how light, CO₂ and temperature limit the rate
Describe an investigation using pondweed
successCriteria: All: write the word equation
Most: balanced equation and explain limiting factors
Some: design and evaluate the pondweed investigation and read graphs
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: balancing equations; Geography: food security
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on how plants turn sunlight into food for all life; stewardship of crops

keywords.def: process in which plants use light energy to make glucose from CO₂ and water
green pigment that absorbs light energy
the factor in shortest supply that restricts the rate of a process
how quickly something happens, e.g. bubbles per minute

starter: Bismillah. Name the green pigment in chloroplasts.
What is the formula for carbon dioxide?
What is an enzyme?

teach.heading: The equations
bullets: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
Light energy absorbed by chlorophyll
6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
teach.note: Say that light energy is not a reactant but it is written over the arrow. Check balancing: 6 C, 12 H, 18 O on each side. Ask what happens to the glucose: respiration, starch for storage, cellulose for cell walls, lipids in seeds, amino acids with nitrate.
cycle: Water arrives from roots via xylem
Oxygen leaves; glucose is used or stored

teach.heading: Limiting factors
bullets: Light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature
The factor in shortest supply sets the rate
At high temperatures enzymes denature
teach.note: Use the 'queue at the till' analogy: more tills do not help if you are waiting on a stock-check. Temperature beyond about 45 degrees Celsius denatures the enzymes of photosynthesis, so the rate falls.

teach.heading: Model: pondweed data
bullets: Count bubbles per minute at set distances
Control temperature with a water-bath screen
teach.note: Method: pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, lamp at measured distance, wait 2 minutes, count bubbles for 1 minute, repeat three times and average. Variables: independent is distance; dependent is bubbles per minute; control CO₂, temperature, same piece of weed. Safety: keep the lamp and mains away from water.

model.problem: Mean bubbles per minute at lamp distances: 10 cm: 48, 20 cm: 30, 30 cm: 18, 40 cm: 10. Describe the trend and give a reason.
steps: Read the values as the lamp moves away
Rate falls from 48 to 10 as distance increases
Greater distance means lower light intensity
Light is the limiting factor, so photosynthesis slows
model.answer: As the lamp moves further away, light intensity falls and the rate of photosynthesis decreases.

teach.heading: Reading limiting-factor graphs
bullets: Rising section: the plotted factor is limiting
Flat section: another factor is limiting
teach.note: Ask: at the plateau, what could you change to raise the rate? Pupils must name a different factor from the one on the x-axis.

misconception.wrong: At the flat part of the graph, adding more of the plotted factor will keep raising the rate.
misconception.right: At the plateau another factor is limiting, so only changing that factor will raise the rate.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. At the plateau in bright light, light is not limiting and CO₂ has stopped limiting; at 10 °C enzymes are slow, so temperature is. Pupils who pick light have misread 'bright'.

check.q: A plant in bright light at 10 °C has a photosynthesis rate that levels off as CO₂ concentration rises above 0.10%. What is probably limiting the rate now?
check.why: Light is already bright and CO₂ is no longer limiting at the plateau, so the low temperature (slow enzymes) is limiting.

practice: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis and count atoms on each side.
Why does the pondweed need sodium hydrogencarbonate in the water?
Name three control variables for the lamp-distance investigation.
independent: Core: Use the data to plot rate against distance and describe the pattern.
Extend: A grower raises CO₂ in a glasshouse but yield does not rise. Give two possible reasons. [2 marks]
Stretch: Design a plan to find out whether green light is used as well as red light. [4 marks]
exit: State the three limiting factors. [3 marks]
Return to the big question: how could a farmer decide which factor to raise?
lessons.homework: Learn the word and symbol equations; do 6 questions on limiting factor graphs.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: equation strips to sequence. Stretch: explain light intensity and distance using the inverse relationship.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Leaf structure, gas exchange in plants and mineral ions
lessons.bigQuestion: How is a leaf built like a tiny factory?
objectives: Describe the structure of a leaf and link it to function
Explain gas exchange in plants in light and dark
State the roles of nitrate and magnesium ions and the effects of deficiency
successCriteria: All: label a leaf section
Most: explain adaptations and net gas exchange
Some: interpret hydrogencarbonate indicator results and starch tests
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: pH indicators; Agriculture: fertilisers
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the quiet design of a leaf; moderation in fertiliser use as part of stewardship

keywords.def: pores in the leaf surface that let gases in and out
tightly packed cells at the top of a leaf with many chloroplasts
cell that opens and closes a stoma
needed to make chlorophyll

starter: Bismillah. Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
Name two limiting factors of photosynthesis.
What does a xylem vessel carry?

teach.heading: Inside a leaf
bullets: Waxy cuticle reduces water loss
Palisade layer is near the light and full of chloroplasts
Spongy mesophyll has air spaces for gas diffusion
teach.note: Draw on the board a cross-section top to bottom: cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll with air spaces, lower epidermis with stomata and guard cells; xylem and phloem in the vein. Ask why most stomata are on the lower surface (cooler, less water loss).

head: Part
Adaptation
Function
rows: lets light reach the palisade layer
CO₂ in, O₂ and water vapour out

teach.heading: Gas exchange in light and dark
bullets: Day: photosynthesis is faster than respiration
Net result: CO₂ taken in, O₂ released
Night: only respiration, so O₂ in, CO₂ out
teach.note: Emphasise that plants respire all the time. Hydrogencarbonate indicator: red at normal CO₂, yellow if CO₂ rises, purple if CO₂ falls. Leaf in light turns purple; leaf in dark turns yellow; tube with no leaf stays red (control).

teach.heading: Model: explain an adaptation
bullets: Name the feature
Say what it does
Link to the function
teach.note: Model the three-part pattern: feature, effect, link. Pupils then reuse it in practice.

model.problem: Explain how the palisade layer is adapted for photosynthesis. [3 marks]
steps: Feature: cells are tightly packed at the top of the leaf
Effect: they absorb the most light as it enters
Feature: they contain many chloroplasts with chlorophyll
Link: so more light energy is absorbed for photosynthesis
model.answer: Packed near the surface with many chloroplasts, they absorb most light, so the rate of photosynthesis is high.

teach.heading: Mineral ions and the starch test
bullets: Nitrate makes amino acids and proteins
Magnesium makes chlorophyll
Deficiency: yellow leaves; nitrate also gives stunted growth
teach.note: Starch test: boil leaf 1 minute (stops reactions), hot ethanol in a water bath with no naked flame (removes chlorophyll), rinse in warm water, add iodine. Blue-black means starch. Variegated and foil-covered leaves show chlorophyll and light are needed.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils choose red ('no change') or purple ('it is a leaf'). In the dark there is only respiration, so CO₂ builds up and the indicator goes yellow.

check.q: A leaf in a tube with hydrogencarbonate indicator is wrapped in foil for 2 hours. The indicator is most likely to turn:
check.why: With no light there is no photosynthesis. Respiration releases CO₂, so the indicator turns yellow.

practice: Label the layers of a leaf from top to bottom.
Why does a leaf in the dark still use oxygen?
A farmer sees yellow leaves and stunted growth. Which ion might be short?
independent: Core: Explain how the leaf is adapted for gas exchange. [3 marks]
Extend: Explain why a variegated leaf with a white edge shows no starch there. [2 marks]
Stretch: A plant in a sealed bottle stays alive for months in light. Explain, using gas exchange. [4 marks]
exit: State the function of stomata and of guard cells. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: pick one part of the leaf factory and justify its design.
lessons.homework: Draw and annotate a leaf cross-section from memory.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: annotate a pre-drawn diagram. Stretch: how does a guard cell open the stoma?

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Transport in plants: xylem, phloem and transpiration
lessons.bigQuestion: How does water climb a 50-metre tree with no pump?
objectives: Describe the roles of xylem and phloem
Explain transpiration and the factors that affect it
Describe the potometer investigation and calculate a rate
successCriteria: All: state what xylem and phloem carry
Most: explain transpiration and its factors
Some: calculate the volume of water lost using a potometer
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: evaporation; Maths: volume of a cylinder
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at unseen processes; stewardship of water

keywords.def: dead hollow tubes carrying water and mineral ions up the plant
living tubes carrying sucrose and amino acids to where needed
loss of water vapour from the leaves, mainly through the stomata
apparatus that measures water uptake by a shoot

starter: Bismillah. What is osmosis?
Name the process by which mineral ions enter root hair cells against a gradient.
What do guard cells control?

teach.heading: Two transport tissues
bullets: Xylem: water and mineral ions, root to leaf
Phloem: sucrose and amino acids, to growing and storage regions
Xylem is dead with lignin; phloem is living
teach.note: Distinguish translocation (phloem) from transpiration (water loss). Pupils frequently swap the two vessels. Root hair cells have a large surface area; water enters by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport.

left.title: Xylem
points: Hollow, dead cells strengthened with lignin

teach.heading: Transpiration
bullets: Water evaporates from leaf cells into air spaces
Water vapour diffuses out through open stomata
Water is pulled up the xylem to replace it
teach.note: This is the transpiration stream. Benefits: brings minerals, cools the leaf, keeps cells turgid. If water loss exceeds uptake the plant wilts.

head: Factor
Effect on transpiration
Reason
rows: removes humid air at the leaf

teach.heading: Model: potometer calculation
bullets: Volume = π × r² × distance
Rate = volume ÷ time
teach.note: Reinforce: measure the bubble position at the start and after a fixed time; cut the shoot under water to avoid air locks; make joints airtight; allow the shoot to equilibrate. Repeat for different conditions with a fan, or in the dark.

model.problem: In a potometer a bubble moves 24 mm in 10 minutes. The capillary tube has radius 0.5 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ per minute.
steps: Volume = π × 0.5² × 24
= 1.9 mm³ per minute (2 s.f.)
model.answer: 1.9 mm³ per minute

teach.heading: Water uptake is not the same as transpiration
bullets: Most water absorbed is lost
A little is used in photosynthesis and for turgor
teach.note: Tell pupils a potometer measures uptake, a close estimate of transpiration. Always state this assumption when evaluating.

misconception.wrong: A potometer measures the exact rate of transpiration.
misconception.right: It measures water uptake, which is only an estimate of transpiration because some water is used in photosynthesis and cell turgor.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils think humid air speeds transpiration; high humidity shrinks the concentration gradient and slows it.

check.q: Which conditions give the highest rate of transpiration?
check.why: Heat speeds evaporation, dry air keeps a steep concentration gradient, and wind removes humid air around the leaf.

practice: State which tissue transports sucrose and which transports water.
Explain why a plant wilts on a hot, windy day.
A bubble moves 30 mm in 15 minutes in a capillary of radius 0.5 mm. Calculate the rate in mm³ per minute.
independent: Core: Describe how you would test the effect of wind on transpiration with a potometer.
Extend: Explain why the volume of water lost is not an exact measure of transpiration. [2 marks]
Stretch: Explain, with reference to stomata, why plants lose less water at night. [3 marks]
exit: Give two differences between xylem and phloem. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: explain how water reaches the top of a tree.
lessons.homework: Draw a flow diagram of the transpiration stream and add three factors.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sentence starters for the stream. Stretch: why is a plant with a thick cuticle better suited to a desert?

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Human diet, digestion, bile and the villus
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a sandwich become part of you?
objectives: Describe a balanced diet and the roles of nutrients
Describe the action of digestive enzymes and bile
Explain how the villus is adapted for absorption
successCriteria: All: list nutrients and the enzymes
Most: explain bile and enzyme action
Some: explain absorption using surface area and concentration gradients
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: nutrition and performance; Chemistry: pH
lessons.smsc: Moral: halal, tayyib and moderation in eating; gratitude for food

keywords.def: diet containing the right amounts of all nutrients for health
break fat into small droplets, increasing surface area
finger-like projection of the small intestine wall that absorbs food
wave of muscle contraction that pushes food along the gut

starter: Bismillah. Name the food test for starch and the colour for a positive result.
What is an enzyme?
State the effect of high temperature on an enzyme.

teach.heading: A balanced diet
bullets: Carbohydrates and lipids give energy
Protein for growth and repair
Vitamins and minerals for health; fibre; water
teach.note: Link to the Year 10 food tests lesson. Keep deficiencies concrete: vitamin C (scurvy), vitamin D with calcium (rickets, weak bones), iron (anaemia, low haemoglobin), fibre (prevents constipation). Energy needs vary with age, activity and pregnancy.

teach.heading: Enzymes of digestion
bullets: Amylase: starch → maltose, then maltase → glucose
Protease: protein → amino acids
Lipase: lipid → fatty acids + glycerol
teach.note: Amylase is made in the salivary glands and pancreas; protease (pepsin) works in the stomach at about pH 2; lipase and other enzymes work in the small intestine at about pH 8. Ask why the optimum pH differs.

teach.heading: Bile
bullets: Made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder
Alkaline: neutralises stomach acid
Emulsifies fat: more surface area for lipase
teach.note: Bile contains no enzymes. It does not digest fat chemically; it breaks it into droplets so lipase can work faster.

model.problem: Explain the role of bile in digestion. [3 marks]
steps: Bile is alkaline so it neutralises acid from the stomach
This gives the right pH for enzymes in the small intestine
It emulsifies fats into small droplets
So a larger surface area is available for lipase
model.answer: Neutralises acid and emulsifies fats, speeding up fat digestion.

teach.heading: The villus
bullets: Thin wall one cell thick
Rich capillary network and a lacteal
Large surface area from villi and microvilli
teach.note: Link to diffusion and active transport: glucose and amino acids move into blood by diffusion and active transport; fatty acids and glycerol enter the lacteal. A steep concentration gradient is kept by blood flow carrying nutrients away.

misconception.wrong: Nutrients are absorbed by diffusion only, so no energy is needed.
misconception.right: Glucose and amino acids also use active transport, which needs energy from respiration, especially when the gut concentration is lower than in the blood.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils pick the stomach because of acid. Bile is made in the liver and only stored in the gall bladder.

check.q: Where is bile made?
check.why: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

practice: Name the enzyme that digests starch and the product.
Explain why protease in the stomach has a different optimum pH from lipase in the small intestine.
State two adaptations of a villus.
independent: Core: Make a flow chart of the digestive system with an enzyme at each site.
Extend: A patient has their gall bladder removed. Predict and explain the effect on fat digestion. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why a lacteal and a capillary network are both needed in a villus. [3 marks]
exit: Name one nutrient, its use and a deficiency effect. [3 marks]
Return to the big question: describe the journey of one slice of bread.
lessons.homework: Design a balanced menu for a day with two nutrients identified per meal.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: diagram labelling with word bank. Stretch: compare absorption by diffusion and active transport.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Respiration: ATP, aerobic and anaerobic
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do your muscles burn when you sprint, and why does bread rise?
objectives: Describe respiration as the release of energy to make ATP
Write equations for aerobic and anaerobic respiration
Describe a yeast investigation and explain results
successCriteria: All: write the word equation for aerobic respiration
Most: compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscle and yeast
Some: analyse temperature data from the yeast practical
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: exothermic reactions; Food technology: bread and brewing
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude for the energy that sustains the body; moderation in exertion

keywords.def: chemical reactions in cells that release energy from nutrient molecules
molecule that stores and transfers energy for cell processes
release of energy from glucose without oxygen
anaerobic respiration in yeast giving ethanol and carbon dioxide

starter: Bismillah. Name the organelle where aerobic respiration happens.
State two uses of glucose in a plant.
Write the formula of oxygen and of carbon dioxide.

teach.heading: Why respire?
bullets: Respiration is not breathing
It transfers energy from glucose to ATP
ATP is used for movement, growth, active transport, heat
teach.note: Ask: is breathing the same as respiration? Break the misconception early. Think of ATP as the small change of the cell: glucose is the banknote, ATP the coins you can spend anywhere in the cell.

left.title: Aerobic
points: Releases a lot of energy (about 30 ATP per glucose)

right.title: Anaerobic
points: Releases far less energy (2 ATP per glucose)

teach.heading: Equations
bullets: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
Yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
Muscle: glucose → lactic acid
teach.note: Compare with photosynthesis: aerobic respiration is almost the reverse. Ethanol is C₂H₅OH. Yeast fermentation makes bread rise (CO₂ bubbles) and is the basis of brewing, which pupils may meet in food science.

teach.heading: Model: oxygen debt
bullets: Link observation to anaerobic respiration
Say why breathing stays fast afterwards
teach.note: Elicit that lactic acid is toxic in large amounts and is broken down in the liver using oxygen. This extra oxygen is the oxygen debt.

model.problem: A sprinter breathes heavily for 5 minutes after a race. Explain why. [3 marks]
steps: During the sprint, muscles respire anaerobically as oxygen supply is too slow
Lactic acid builds up
After the race extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid
So breathing rate and depth stay high until it is removed
model.answer: Extra oxygen is needed to remove lactic acid built up by anaerobic respiration.

teach.heading: Practical: yeast and temperature
bullets: Yeast, glucose solution and a gas syringe
Count bubbles or measure CO₂ volume in 5 minutes
Change the temperature of the water bath
teach.note: Variables: independent is temperature (20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C); dependent is bubbles per minute; control yeast mass, glucose concentration, volume. Example mean results (bubbles per minute): 20 °C: 14; 30 °C: 32; 40 °C: 55; 50 °C: 20; 60 °C: 0. Ask pupils to explain the peak at 40 and zero at 60 (enzymes denature). Safety: hot water, goggles.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: lactic acid is the product in human muscle, not in yeast.

check.q: Which products are made when yeast respires anaerobically?
check.why: Yeast fermentation gives ethanol and carbon dioxide. Lactic acid is produced in animal muscle.

practice: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
State where lactic acid is made.
Why does bread dough rise when yeast is added?
independent: Core: Plot the yeast data and describe the trend.
Extend: Explain the shape of the graph using enzymes. [4 marks]
Stretch: Explain why anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose than aerobic. [2 marks]
exit: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration. [2 marks]
Return to the big question in two sentences.
lessons.homework: Make a comparison table of aerobic respiration, muscle anaerobic respiration and yeast fermentation.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: matching cards for products. Stretch: describe how a respirometer with soda lime measures oxygen uptake of germinating seeds.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Breathing and gas exchange in humans
lessons.bigQuestion: How does air get from the nose to the blood, and why is the lung built like a tree?
objectives: Explain inhalation and exhalation using ribs, intercostal muscles and diaphragm
Describe how alveoli are adapted for gas exchange
Compare inhaled and exhaled air and describe a breathing investigation
successCriteria: All: label the thorax and say what the diaphragm does
Most: explain pressure and volume changes
Some: calculate ventilation rate and analyse exercise data
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: pressure and volume; PE: exercise
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the body as an amanah (trust), avoiding harm such as smoking

keywords.def: tiny air sac in the lung where gas exchange takes place
sheet of muscle below the lungs that helps breathing
muscles between the ribs
volume of air breathed per minute

starter: Bismillah. What process releases energy from glucose?
Which gas is produced in respiration?
Define diffusion.

teach.heading: Breathing in and out
bullets: Inhale: intercostals and diaphragm contract
Rib cage up and out, diaphragm flattens
Volume rises, pressure falls, air flows in
teach.note: Use a bell jar model if available. On exhaling the muscles relax, volume falls, pressure rises, air is pushed out. Forced exhalation uses internal intercostals. Pupils often say the lungs 'suck' air; air moves because of a pressure difference.

teach.heading: Alveoli
bullets: Walls one cell thick; moist lining
Surrounded by a dense capillary network
Huge surface area; ventilation keeps gradient steep
teach.note: Oxygen diffuses from alveolus to blood; carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. Blood flow carries oxygen away to keep the gradient. About 300 million alveoli per lung gives a surface area close to the size of a tennis court. Smoking: tar damages alveoli and cilia (optional).

teach.heading: Model: ventilation rate
bullets: Ventilation rate = breaths per minute × tidal volume
Compare rest and exercise
teach.note: Remind pupils that tidal volume is the volume per breath (about 500 cm³ at rest). Core practical idea: count breaths in 1 minute at rest, then after 2 minutes of step-ups, then time how long to return to resting rate; repeat three times.

model.problem: At rest a pupil breathes 15 times per minute with a tidal volume of 500 cm³. After exercise: 28 breaths per minute, 1100 cm³. How many times greater is the ventilation rate after exercise?
steps: Rest: 15 × 500 = 7500 cm³ per minute
Exercise: 28 × 1100 = 30 800 cm³ per minute
model.answer: About 4.1 times greater

teach.heading: Exhaled air test
bullets: Limewater turns milky with more CO₂
Compare breathing through two bottles
teach.note: Set up two boiler tubes of limewater with valves so that you inhale through one and exhale through the other. The exhaled-air tube goes milky faster. Safety: use clean mouthpieces; do not suck up limewater; wash hands.

misconception.wrong: We breathe out only carbon dioxide and breathe in only oxygen.
misconception.right: Inhaled air has 21% oxygen and exhaled air still has 16%; carbon dioxide rises from 0.04% to about 4%.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils say pressure rises as volume rises. Air moves from high to low pressure, so pressure must fall for air to enter.

check.q: During inhalation, what happens to the pressure in the chest?
check.why: The chest volume increases so the pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in.

practice: List the steps of exhalation in order.
Give three adaptations of alveoli.
A pupil breathes 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 450 cm³. Calculate the ventilation rate.
independent: Core: Describe how you would investigate the effect of exercise on breathing rate.
Extend: Explain why breathing rate stays high for several minutes after exercise. [3 marks]
Stretch: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls. Explain the effect on gas exchange. [3 marks]
exit: Compare inhaled and exhaled air in one sentence for oxygen and for CO₂. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: link tree-like branching to surface area.
lessons.homework: Annotate a diagram of the thorax; learn the table of inhalation and exhalation.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: act out the rib movements; label cards. Stretch: why is breathing at altitude harder?

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Blood and the immune system
lessons.bigQuestion: How does your body remember an illness it has met only once?
objectives: State the functions of the four components of blood
Explain how white blood cells defend the body
Explain how vaccination gives immunity
successCriteria: All: name blood components and functions
Most: describe phagocytes, antibodies and vaccination
Some: interpret primary and secondary response graphs
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: public health; History: smallpox
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting others through vaccination; trust in medical science and care for the community (hifz al-nafs)

keywords.def: molecule on a pathogen that triggers an immune response
protein made by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen
white blood cell that engulfs pathogens
giving a harmless form of antigen so the body makes memory cells

starter: Bismillah. Name the four types of pathogen.
State one adaptation of a red blood cell.
What does a virus need to reproduce?

teach.heading: What is in blood?
bullets: Plasma carries CO₂, nutrients, urea, hormones and heat
Red cells carry oxygen as oxyhaemoglobin
Platelets help clots form
teach.note: Red cells: biconcave disc (large surface area), no nucleus (more room for haemoglobin). White cells: phagocytes and lymphocytes. Platelets form a clot and scab, sealing wounds and keeping microbes out.

teach.heading: How white blood cells defend
bullets: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens
Lymphocytes make antibodies specific to an antigen
Antitoxins neutralise toxins released by pathogens
teach.note: Use a lock-and-key analogy: each antibody has a shape that fits one antigen only. After infection, memory lymphocytes remain, so a second infection by the same pathogen is dealt with faster.

teach.heading: Model: vaccination graph
bullets: Read the first and second peaks
State the difference in speed and size
teach.note: Take the data from a case: first injection at day 0, peak 20 units at day 14. Booster at day 28, peak 180 units at day 33. Ask what has changed (memory cells, faster, bigger).

model.problem: Antibody level after a first injection peaks at 20 units on day 14. After a booster on day 28 it peaks at 180 units on day 33. Compare the two responses.
steps: First response: 14 days to reach peak, 20 units
Second response: 5 days to reach peak, 180 units
180 ÷ 20 = 9 times higher
Memory cells made the second response faster and larger
model.answer: The second response is 9 times larger and 9 days faster because of memory cells.

teach.heading: Vaccination: what and why
bullets: Dead or weakened pathogen, or just antigens
Body makes antibodies and memory cells
Future infection is stopped quickly
teach.note: Be accurate: a vaccine contains antigens, not antibodies. The person does not get ill because the pathogen is harmless. Many parents ask about safety; refer to NHS guidance and the school nurse for questions.

misconception.wrong: A vaccine gives you antibodies straight away.
misconception.right: A vaccine contains harmless antigens. Your own lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer D. Trap: pupils pick phagocytes because they 'fight' pathogens; phagocytes engulf, lymphocytes make antibodies.

check.q: Which cells make antibodies?
check.why: Lymphocytes make antibodies. Phagocytes engulf pathogens; red cells carry oxygen; platelets clot blood.

practice: State the function of each of the four blood components.
Why are red blood cells biconcave?
Explain why antibodies for one disease do not work on another pathogen.
independent: Core: Describe in order what happens when pathogens enter a cut.
Extend: Explain why a person is rarely ill twice from the same chickenpox virus. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why a vaccine is less effective if the pathogen mutates its antigens. [3 marks]
exit: Define antigen and antibody. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: use the term memory cell.
lessons.homework: Draw a storyboard (6 frames) for how a vaccine gives immunity.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: glossary cards with images. Stretch: compare active and passive immunity.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: The heart, blood vessels and coronary heart disease
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can a blocked artery as small as a pencil lead stop the heart?
objectives: Describe the structure of the heart and double circulation
Compare arteries, veins and capillaries
Explain the causes and risk factors of coronary heart disease
successCriteria: All: label the heart and name the vessels
Most: link vessel structure to function
Some: explain coronary heart disease and evaluate risk factors
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: exercise and heart rate; Maths: rates
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for health; moderation (wasatiyyah) in diet and lifestyle

keywords.def: blood passes through the heart twice on each complete circuit
vessel carrying blood away from the heart at high pressure
vessel carrying blood towards the heart; has valves
artery supplying the heart muscle with oxygenated blood

starter: Bismillah. Which blood component carries oxygen?
Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
What does the diaphragm do in inhalation?

teach.heading: The heart and double circulation
bullets: Right side: deoxygenated blood to the lungs
Left side: oxygenated blood to the body
Valves stop backflow; left ventricle wall is thickest
teach.note: Trace one drop of blood: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta. Show a labelled diagram. Heart rate rises with exercise because adrenaline and the brain signal the heart.
cycle: Vena cava brings blood from the body
Pulmonary vein returns to left atrium
Left ventricle pumps blood out through the aorta

teach.heading: Three kinds of vessel
bullets: Arteries: thick, muscular, elastic walls; narrow lumen
Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves
Capillaries: one cell thick for exchange
teach.note: Pupils often say all arteries carry oxygenated blood. Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

teach.heading: Model: structure to function
bullets: Name the feature, the function, then the link
Use data: wall thickness
teach.note: Practice phrasing: the left ventricle pumps to the whole body, the right only to the lungs next door.

model.problem: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the right. [2 marks]
steps: The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, a long way
This needs a higher pressure than pumping to the nearby lungs
A thicker muscular wall contracts more strongly to give that pressure
model.answer: A thicker wall generates the greater pressure needed to pump blood around the body.

teach.heading: Coronary heart disease
bullets: Fatty deposits narrow coronary arteries
Less oxygen reaches heart muscle: chest pain, heart attack
Risk: diet high in saturated fat, smoking, stress, genetics
teach.note: Distinguish risk factors that can be changed (diet, smoking, exercise, stress) from those that cannot (genes, age, sex). Explain that correlation shows association, not proof of cause; link to evaluating data in exam questions.

misconception.wrong: Veins carry deoxygenated blood and arteries carry oxygenated blood, always.
misconception.right: Direction relative to the heart defines them. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer D. Trap: the rule 'arteries carry oxygenated blood' leads pupils to pick the pulmonary artery.

check.q: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
check.why: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

practice: List the heart chambers in the order blood flows through them.
State two adaptations of veins.
Why does the heart muscle need its own blood supply?
independent: Core: Compare the structure of an artery and a vein.
Extend: Heart rate was 68 beats per minute at rest and 142 after exercise. Calculate the percentage increase. [2 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the claim that stress alone causes coronary heart disease. [4 marks]
exit: Describe what happens in the coronary arteries in coronary heart disease. [3 marks]
Return to the big question: link a narrow artery to oxygen and heart muscle.
lessons.homework: Draw a flow diagram of double circulation using two colours for oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded diagram. Stretch: how do stents and statins reduce risk?

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Excretion: lungs, skin and the kidney nephron
lessons.bigQuestion: How do the kidneys clean 180 litres of fluid a day and keep what you need?
objectives: Name excretory organs and the substances they remove
Describe ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption in the nephron
Explain how ADH controls the concentration of urine
successCriteria: All: name organs and waste products
Most: describe the stages of the nephron
Some: interpret filtrate and urine data and ADH feedback
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: solutes; PE: hydration
lessons.smsc: Moral: gratitude; avoiding excess; fasting and hydration awareness as health discussion

keywords.def: removal of toxic waste and excess substances from the body
waste made in the liver from excess amino acids
filtering of small molecules from blood under high pressure
hormone that makes the kidney reabsorb more water

starter: Bismillah. Name the gas produced by respiration that the lungs remove.
What does the pituitary gland make?
Define osmosis.

teach.heading: Excretory organs
bullets: Lungs: carbon dioxide and some water vapour
Skin: sweat has water, salts and a little urea
Kidneys: urea, excess water and ions
teach.note: Urea is made in the liver by deamination (breaking down excess amino acids) and carried in blood plasma to the kidneys. Not the same as egestion (faeces). Typical adult urine output is about 1 to 1.5 litres a day.

teach.heading: Inside the nephron
bullets: Ultrafiltration: water, glucose, urea, ions forced out
Selective reabsorption: all glucose, some water and ions
Remaining fluid is urine
teach.note: Ask: why do proteins and blood cells stay in the blood? (too large to pass through). Glucose is reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal tubule, which is why mitochondria are abundant there. A healthy person has no glucose in the urine.
cycle: Blood enters the glomerulus at high pressure
Small molecules filter into the Bowman's capsule
Urea and extra water leave as urine

teach.heading: Model: interpret data
bullets: Compare plasma, filtrate and urine
Explain each difference
teach.note: Data in g per 100 cm³. Plasma protein 8.0, filtrate 0, urine 0. Glucose 0.10, 0.10, 0. Urea 0.03, 0.03, 2.0.

model.problem: Using the data (protein: 8.0 / 0 / 0; glucose: 0.10 / 0.10 / 0; urea: 0.03 / 0.03 / 2.0 g per 100 cm³ in plasma / filtrate / urine), explain each pattern.
steps: Protein is in plasma only: too large to be filtered
Glucose is in the filtrate but not urine: all reabsorbed by active transport
Urea rises from 0.03 to 2.0: water reabsorbed, so urea is concentrated
Urea is not reabsorbed, so it leaves in urine
model.answer: Large molecules stay in blood; glucose is reabsorbed; urea becomes concentrated in urine.

teach.heading: ADH and water balance
bullets: Dehydrated: more ADH released by the pituitary
Collecting duct becomes more permeable to water
Small volume of concentrated urine
Plenty of water: less ADH, large volume of dilute urine
teach.note: This is negative feedback. Walk through a hot day with no drinks. The blood is more concentrated, so the brain detects this and signals the pituitary gland. Mention dialysis and kidney transplants as treatments for kidney failure; keep it factual and sensitive.

misconception.wrong: ADH makes the body make more urine.
misconception.right: ADH reduces urine volume by making the kidney reabsorb more water, so the urine is more concentrated.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils think more ADH means more urine. Dehydration raises ADH, which increases water reabsorption.

check.q: A student has not drunk for 10 hours. What happens to ADH and urine?
check.why: Dehydration raises ADH, so more water is reabsorbed and urine is concentrated and small in volume.

practice: Name the waste product made in the liver from amino acids.
State where ultrafiltration occurs.
Why is there no glucose in the urine of a healthy person?
independent: Core: Describe the path of a molecule of urea from blood to urine.
Extend: A person drinks 1.5 litres of water quickly. Explain the change in ADH and urine. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why glucose appears in the urine of an untreated person with diabetes. [3 marks]
exit: Name two excretory organs and one substance each excretes. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: where is the cleaning done and where is the keeping done?
lessons.homework: Make a labelled nephron diagram with the four steps in colour.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: flow-chart cards in order. Stretch: how does a dialysis machine mimic the nephron?

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Co-ordination: reflex arc and the eye
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do you pull your hand away before you feel the pain?
objectives: Describe the stimulus, receptor, co-ordinator, effector and response chain
Explain the reflex arc and compare it with a voluntary response
Describe the structure and function of the eye and the pupil reflex
successCriteria: All: sequence a reflex arc
Most: link the structure of the eye to its function
Some: explain the pupil reflex and accommodation
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: light and lenses; PE: reaction times
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on the body's design and gratitude for sight

keywords.def: a change in the environment that is detected
cell or organ that detects a stimulus
muscle or gland that produces a response
pathway from receptor to effector for a rapid automatic response

starter: Bismillah. Name the organ systems in the body that you know.
Which hormone is released from the adrenal glands in danger?
What is the function of a motor neurone?

teach.heading: The nervous pathway
bullets: Stimulus, receptor, co-ordinator, effector, response
Co-ordinator: brain or spinal cord
Neurones carry electrical impulses
teach.note: Walk through touching a hot pan. Introduce sensory, relay and motor neurones. At a synapse, a chemical (neurotransmitter) diffuses across the gap. Reflexes are fast, automatic, and protect the body.

teach.heading: Structure of the eye
bullets: Cornea and lens focus light on the retina
Iris controls the size of the pupil
Optic nerve carries impulses to the brain
teach.note: Labelled diagram on the board. Retina has rod cells (dim light, no colour) and cone cells (colour). The fovea is the most sensitive point. Accommodation: viewing near objects, ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, lens becomes thicker and more curved; for distant objects the reverse. Check specification level for accommodation.

head: Part
Function
rows: refracts light as it enters the eye

teach.heading: Model: the pupil reflex
bullets: Receptors in the retina detect brightness
Muscles in the iris respond
teach.note: Check: circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax in bright light. In dim light the pupil dilates. This protects the retina yet allows vision in the dark.

model.problem: Explain what happens to the pupil when a person walks from a dark room into bright sunlight. [3 marks]
steps: Light receptors in the retina detect the bright light
Impulses go to the brain and back to the iris muscles
Circular muscles contract, radial muscles relax
The pupil gets smaller, reducing light that reaches the retina and avoiding damage
model.answer: The pupil constricts to protect the retina.

teach.heading: Reaction time practice
bullets: Ruler-drop test
Distance dropped gives time: t = √(2d ÷ g)
teach.note: Example: a mean drop of 18 cm gives t = √(2 × 0.18 ÷ 9.8) = 0.19 s. Variables: same ruler, hand, no warning. A voluntary response involves the brain deciding; a reflex does not, so it is faster.

misconception.wrong: Reflexes are controlled by the brain.
misconception.right: Reflex responses are coordinated by the spinal cord (or lower brain) without conscious thought, so they are faster.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils pick the sensory neurone because it starts the reflex; the motor neurone reaches the effector.

check.q: In a reflex arc, which neurone carries the impulse to the muscle?
check.why: Motor neurones carry impulses to effectors. Sensory neurones go to the spinal cord and relay neurones link them.

practice: Put the five terms of the nervous pathway in order.
State the function of the retina.
Name the effector in the hot-pan reflex.
independent: Core: Label a diagram of the eye and write one function for each part.
Extend: Explain why a reflex is faster than a voluntary action. [2 marks]
Stretch: Explain what happens in the eye when focusing on a book after looking at a distant tree. [4 marks]
exit: State what happens at a synapse. [2 marks]
Return to the big question using the reflex arc.
lessons.homework: Write a short story of a reflex using all six key terms.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequencing cards. Stretch: how does colour vision work through cone cells?

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Hormones and plant responses
lessons.bigQuestion: How do chemical messengers in plants and people coordinate responses?
objectives: Describe hormones and compare nervous and hormonal control
State the roles of adrenaline, insulin, testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone
Explain phototropism and gravitropism using auxin
successCriteria: All: name hormones and glands
Most: explain adrenaline's effects and compare with nerves
Some: explain tropisms with auxin and interpret experiments
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: chemical messengers; Geography: farming practice
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: unseen messengers in plants and people as signs of order

keywords.def: chemical messenger made in a gland and carried in the blood
organ that responds to a particular hormone
plant hormone controlling growth by cell elongation
growth response of a plant to a directional stimulus

starter: Bismillah. Name the three neurones in a reflex arc.
What is a gland?
Define stimulus.

teach.heading: Hormones in humans
bullets: Made in endocrine glands, carried in the blood
Act on target organs
Slower and longer lasting than nerves
teach.note: Compare with the nervous system: electrical, very fast, short-lived, precise. Adrenaline (adrenal glands) prepares for fight or flight: increased heart rate, more glucose released, wider airways, pupils dilate.

teach.heading: Nerves versus hormones
bullets: Speed of response is very different
Duration of effect differs
Route: neurones or blood
teach.note: Hinge idea: choose a stimulus (hot pan, exam stress) and ask which system is used.

teach.heading: Model: phototropism
bullets: Auxin is made in the shoot tip
Light causes auxin to move to the shaded side
Cells there elongate more, so the shoot bends towards light
teach.note: Experiments: cover the tip with foil (no bending), remove the tip (no growth), light from one side with an intact tip (bends). In gravitropism shoots grow upwards, roots grow downwards. Auxin is unequally distributed.

model.problem: A seedling with its tip removed is lit from the right. Predict and explain the result. [3 marks]
steps: The tip makes auxin
With the tip gone, no auxin is made
No auxin to elongate cells, so little or no growth
No bending toward light
model.answer: It does not grow or bend, because no auxin is produced.

teach.heading: Why plants matter to farmers
bullets: Auxin used in rooting powders
Tropisms keep shoots in light and roots in soil
teach.note: Make the link to farming. Some pupils say plants 'know' where light is; stress that unequal auxin distribution is the mechanism.

misconception.wrong: Plants bend towards light because the cells on the lit side grow more.
misconception.right: Auxin moves to the shaded side, where cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: shoots grow against gravity (negative gravitropism); roots grow with gravity. No light is involved here.

check.q: A seedling is laid on its side in the dark. The shoot grows upwards. This is called:
check.why: The shoot grows against the direction of gravity, so this is negative gravitropism.

practice: Name the gland that makes insulin and the hormone released in fear.
Give two differences between nervous and hormonal control.
Where is auxin made in a shoot?
independent: Core: Make a table of five hormones, their glands and effects.
Extend: Explain why a fox that sees a hunter has a faster heart rate in seconds yet needs minutes to calm down. [3 marks]
Stretch: Design an experiment to show the shoot tip detects light. [4 marks]
exit: State two effects of adrenaline. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: one example in a plant and one in a person.
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled diagram showing auxin movement in a shoot lit from the left.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: matching hormone-effect cards. Stretch: why do roots respond differently to auxin?

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Homeostasis: blood glucose and body temperature
lessons.bigQuestion: How does your body keep inside the same when outside changes?
objectives: Define homeostasis and negative feedback
Explain how insulin controls blood glucose and what goes wrong in diabetes
Explain skin responses to heat and cold
successCriteria: All: define homeostasis
Most: explain the control of blood glucose and temperature
Some: interpret graphs and avoid common errors about capillaries
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: exercise and heat; Physics: heat transfer
lessons.smsc: Moral: the amanah of the body; moderation in sugar intake

keywords.def: maintaining a constant internal environment
change is detected and the response reverses it
widening of arterioles supplying skin capillaries
narrowing of arterioles supplying skin capillaries

starter: Bismillah. Name two hormones and their glands.
What is the normal core body temperature?
What does the pancreas make?

teach.heading: Negative feedback
bullets: Receptor detects a change from the set point
Control centre triggers an effector
The response reverses the change
teach.note: Use the thermostat analogy. Body core temperature is about 37 °C; the brain monitors blood temperature, and skin receptors detect external conditions.
cycle: Receptors in skin and brain detect it

teach.heading: Blood glucose
bullets: After a meal glucose rises; pancreas releases insulin
Liver converts glucose to glycogen
Blood glucose returns to normal
teach.note: Type 1 diabetes: the pancreas makes little or no insulin; treatment is insulin injections, diet and monitoring. Type 2: body cells respond poorly to insulin; managed by diet and exercise. Glucagon (stretch): released when glucose is low, converts glycogen to glucose.

teach.heading: Model: skin and temperature
bullets: Name the response
Say what it changes
Say why this restores temperature
teach.note: Use the misconception to follow. Capillaries cannot move; arterioles widen or narrow. Shivering is rapid muscle contraction releasing heat from respiration. Hair erect traps a layer of air, though pupils will rightly note humans have little body hair.

model.problem: Explain why a person's skin looks red and sweaty after running. [3 marks]
steps: Body temperature rises during exercise
Arterioles in the skin widen (vasodilation), more blood flows near the surface
More heat is lost by radiation, so the skin looks red
Sweat evaporates and removes heat from the skin
model.answer: Vasodilation and sweating lose heat to bring temperature down.

teach.heading: A very common mistake
bullets: Skin blood vessels do not move
Arterioles change their diameter
teach.note: Say this slowly: the vessels do not move towards or away from the surface.

misconception.wrong: When hot, capillaries move closer to the skin surface.
misconception.right: Capillaries cannot move. Arterioles supplying them widen (vasodilation), so more blood flows through skin capillaries.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils think shivering cools you. It releases heat from muscle respiration.

check.q: Which response helps warm a cold person?
check.why: Shivering releases heat from respiration in muscle; vasodilation and sweating cool the body.

practice: Define negative feedback.
State what insulin does.
Describe two responses when body temperature falls.
independent: Core: Use the glucose data to describe differences between the two people.
Extend: Explain why an insulin injection must be matched to food intake. [3 marks]
Stretch: Compare the control of blood glucose with the control of temperature, identifying receptor, effector, response. [4 marks]
exit: Define homeostasis. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: choose one variable and explain how it is kept steady.
lessons.homework: Draw a negative feedback loop for blood glucose and one for temperature.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sentence frames for feedback loops. Stretch: how do continuous glucose monitors work?

lessons.title: Solutions, solubility curves and diffusion of gases
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a hot drink dissolve more sugar than a cold one, and what happens when it cools?
objectives: Use the terms solute, solvent, solution and saturated solution
Read and use solubility curves
Explain gas diffusion using particles and relative molecular mass
successCriteria: All: define the key terms
Most: read a solubility curve
